# Ch. 5: Stream live clicks


Real-time delivery means pushing data to whoever is listening the moment it changes, like a live
click counter on a dashboard. On iii that is what observing a function does: `worker.observe(a, b)`
runs `b` each time `a` runs. A live click feed is a function that runs once per click, and anyone
who wants to hear about clicks observes it, the same way you observed `http::on-request` and
`queue::on-message` in earlier chapters. You'll give the feed to a dedicated `click-streamer` worker
so the `link` worker stays focused on links.

A notification is not storage. The clicks already live in the `clicks` table from Chapter 3, so a
listener that joins late reads the current total with a query, then counts the notifications that
follow.

<Note>
  Earlier versions of this chapter used `iii-stream` and `pubsub`. If your project still has them,
  see [Migrate from iii-stream and pubsub](../../upgrading/migrate-from-streams).
</Note>

## Add the worker

The `click-streamer` worker owns the live click feed. Uncomment the Ch. 5 block under `containers`:

```yaml worker-compose.yaml
click-streamer:
  worker: path://./click-streamer
```

## Host the click feed in `click-streamer`

The feed is `click-streamer::on-click`, a function that runs once per recorded click and returns
that click. What a function returns is what its observers receive, so every listener gets
`{ id, code, clicked_at }` for each click. `click-streamer` runs the feed each time
`link::record_click` runs, by observing it.

Create `click-streamer/src/index.ts`:

```typescript click-streamer/src/index.ts
import { ObserveRejection, registerWorker } from "iii-sdk";
import { Logger } from "@iii-dev/helpers/observability";

const worker = registerWorker(process.env.III_URL ?? "ws://localhost:49134", {
  workerName: "click-streamer",
});
const logger = new Logger();

type Click = { id: number; code: string; clicked_at: string };

// The live feed. Each call is one click, and the click it returns is what
// every listener receives.
const onClick = worker.registerFunction(
  "click-streamer::on-click",
  async (click: Click): Promise<Click> => ({
    id: click.id,
    code: click.code,
    clicked_at: click.clicked_at,
  }),
  {
    description: "Runs once per recorded click. Observers receive { id, code, clicked_at }.",
    // Only click-streamer calls the feed. Any worker may observe it.
    private: true,
  },
);

// iii accepts every observer by default. Cap the listeners: a throw rejects
// the new observer, and the worker that asked sees the error.
const MAX_LISTENERS = 256;
onClick.onObserverAdded(() => {
  if (onClick.observers().length >= MAX_LISTENERS) {
    throw new ObserveRejection(
      "TOO_MANY_LISTENERS",
      "click-streamer::on-click: too many listeners",
    );
  }
});

// Runs each time link::record_click runs, with the click it returned.
worker.registerFunction("click-streamer::announce", async (click: Click) => {
  await worker.call({ function_id: "click-streamer::on-click", payload: click });
  return null;
});
worker.observe(
  { function_id: "link::record_click", deliver: "output" },
  "click-streamer::announce",
);

logger.info("click-streamer ready");
```

Each part of that file has one job:

- **The feed returns the click.** `click-streamer::on-click` builds the click from the three fields
  a listener needs and returns it. Its observers receive that value.
- **Only `click-streamer` calls the feed.** `private: true` makes the engine accept calls of
  `click-streamer::on-click` from its own worker only, so no other worker can announce a click that
  never happened. Other workers can still observe it, which matters in Chapter 7, when a browser tab
  observes it.
- **The listeners are capped.** `onObserverAdded` runs before iii accepts a new observer of the
  feed, and overrides iii's default of accepting every one: past 256 listeners it throws, and the
  observer is rejected.
- **`announce` connects the feed to `link`.** It observes `link::record_click` with
  `deliver: "output"`, so it runs after each successful call of `link::record_click` and receives
  what that call returned. It then calls the feed with the click.

## Return the click from `link`

`click-streamer::announce` receives what `link::record_click` returns, so have it return the click
it recorded. `database::execute` returns the new row's id as `last_insert_id`; it travels with the
click so listeners can tell a new click from one they have already counted. Replace
`link::record_click` in `link/src/index.ts`:

```typescript link/src/index.ts {4-7,15-16}
worker.registerFunction(
  "link::record_click",
  async (payload: { code: string; clicked_at: string }) => {
    const { last_insert_id } = await worker.call<
      { db: string; sql: string; params: string[] },
      { last_insert_id: string | null }
    >({
      function_id: "database::execute",
      payload: {
        db: DB,
        sql: "INSERT INTO clicks (code, clicked_at) VALUES (?, ?)",
        params: [payload.code, payload.clicked_at],
      },
    });
    // The row is committed. Observers of link::record_click receive this click.
    return { id: Number(last_insert_id), code: payload.code, clicked_at: payload.clicked_at };
  },
);
```

The `link` worker stays focused on links: it records the click and returns it, and `click-streamer`
reacts to that on its own.

<Info>
  A live counter is best effort. iii hands each click to the listeners without waiting for them, so
  the click write never waits on a slow listener, and a click a listener misses is not replayed. The
  listener's next read of the total corrects it.
</Info>

## Read the current total

A listener that connects now has missed every earlier click, and notifications are never replayed.
Give it a query to start from: add `link::click_summary` to `link/src/index.ts`. It returns the
number of clicks and the highest click id, so a listener knows which notifications are already
included in the total.

```typescript link/src/index.ts
worker.registerFunction("link::click_summary", async () => {
  const { rows } = await worker.call<
    { db: string; sql: string },
    { rows: Array<{ total: number; last_id: number | null }> }
  >({
    function_id: "database::query",
    payload: { db: DB, sql: "SELECT COUNT(*) AS total, MAX(id) AS last_id FROM clicks" },
  });
  return { total: rows[0]?.total ?? 0, last_id: rows[0]?.last_id ?? 0 };
});
```

Restart Compose so it picks up the change:

```bash
iii call compose::restart
```

The browser you build in Chapter 7 observes `click-streamer::on-click` and counts clicks live.

## See it work

A listener is any worker that observes `click-streamer::on-click`. The scaffold ships a small one
that prints each click, commented out in `click-streamer/watch.ts`: uncomment its Ch. 5 block (a
fully commented file runs, prints nothing and exits). The code:

```typescript click-streamer/watch.ts
import { registerWorker } from "iii-sdk";

const worker = registerWorker(process.env.III_URL ?? "ws://127.0.0.1:49134", {
  workerName: "click-watcher",
  // The project's namespace, where click-streamer::on-click and link::* live.
  namespace: process.env.III_NAMESPACE || "default",
});

type Click = { id: number; code: string; clicked_at: string };

worker.registerFunction("click-watcher::print", async (click: Click) => {
  console.log(`click #${click.id}: ${click.code} at ${click.clicked_at}`);
  return null;
});

// Observe first, then read the total, so no click falls between the two.
// deliver: "output" hands click-watcher::print the click the feed returned.
await worker
  .observe({ function_id: "click-streamer::on-click", deliver: "output" }, "click-watcher::print")
  .ready();

const summary = await worker.call<Record<string, never>, { total: number; last_id: number }>({
  function_id: "link::click_summary",
  payload: {},
});
console.log(`watching clicks, ${summary.total} recorded so far`);
```

`ready()` resolves once the observer is active, so every click after that line reaches the watcher.

Run it from the `click-streamer` folder and leave it running:

```bash
cd click-streamer && npm install && npx tsx watch.ts
```

In a second terminal, create a few links and follow each:

```bash
for n in $(seq 1 3); do
  curl -s -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3111/links \
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d "{\"url\":\"https://iii.dev\",\"code\":\"stream-$n\"}"
  curl -s -o /dev/null "http://127.0.0.1:3111/s/stream-$n"
done
```

Running the loop again is fine: the links already exist, so `POST /links` answers `409` with
``{"error":"code `stream-1` is already taken"}``, and each redirect still records a new click.
Change the numbers in `seq` to create new links.

Each redirect shows up in the watcher as soon as its click row is written:

```text
watching clicks, 0 recorded so far
click #1: stream-1 at 2026-05-27T10:15:02.114Z
click #2: stream-2 at 2026-05-27T10:15:02.169Z
click #3: stream-3 at 2026-05-27T10:15:02.221Z
```

A listener that wants one link's clicks adds a [filter](/using-iii/observers#filters), and iii runs
its target only for the clicks that match:

```typescript
worker.observe(
  {
    function_id: "click-streamer::on-click",
    filters: { "input.code": { $eq: "stream-1" } },
    deliver: "output",
  },
  "click-watcher::print",
);
```

The total is always one query away:

```bash
iii call link::click_summary
```

```json
{ "total": 3, "last_id": 3 }
```

Stop the watcher with `Ctrl+C`. Its observer is suspended when the watcher disconnects, and iii
removes it once the grace period (30 seconds by default) ends without a reconnect.

## Conclusion

Linkly now pushes every click to its listeners in real time: `click-streamer` observes
`link::record_click` and runs its `click-streamer::on-click` feed once per click, and every listener
observes the feed. The `clicks` table stays the source of truth behind `link::click_summary`. Next,
in [Ch. 6: Move bulk data with channels](/tutorials/linkly/channels), you bulk-load links from a CSV
in a single streamed upload.
